To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

SIDS is an inflammatory response to infection, that this response is dysregulated in some individuals, and that the dysregulation can be induced by environmental factors (such as virus infection) or by genetic factors.
SIDS is the result of dysregulation of the inflammatory response to minor infections.

the risk of SIDS increases when infants are exposed to environmental stress (e.g., virus infection, cigarette smoke), and the risk is greater in male infants, in infants with a polymorphic allele that is associated with increased inflammatory responses, and in infants who are in the 2- to-4-month age range.
In summary, our research is concerned with

interactions between genetic factors (cytokine gene polymorphsims) and developmental stage (age-related changes in cortisol levels), and environmental factors (exposure to viruses, cigarette smoke) in the regulation of inflammatory responses.
understanding how the interactions among risk factor genes and environmental factors affect the inflammatory responses of infants and their role in SIDS.
the role of risk factors in the development of inflammatory responses to infectious agents and the role of inflammation in the pathogenesis of SIDS.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the risk factors associated with SIDS are not independent but interact with each other in a complex fashion.

the risk factors for Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) and their role in inflammatory responses to infections are as follows: The risk factors for SIDs are associated with induction and/or suppression of inflammatory responses to minor infections.
the risk factors for Sudden Infant Death Syndrome are associated with induction of inflammatory responses that are dysregulated and result in death.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the risk factors for SUDS are associated with dysregulation of the inflammatory response to infection.
the interactions among genetic, developmental and environmental risk factors are likely to influence inflammatory responses to infections and thus may contribute to the risk of SIDS.
the interactions among genetic and environmental risk factor may explain why some infants succumb to “minor” infection and why others survive.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is no single risk factor that can explain SIDS, but rather that there are a series of risk factors, which, when present together, lead to the death of an infant from a minor infectious disease.
there is no evidence that any one infectious agent is associated consistently with SIDS.

the risk of SIDS is associated with the induction of inflammatory responses by “minor” infections, and that the risk of these infections is increased by exposure to cigarette smoke, virus infections, and other risk factors.
